ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: This study received ethical approval from the Sierra Leone Ethics and Scientific Review Committee of the Ministry of Health, Government of Sierra Leone (referenced SLESRC NO: 012/07/2023) in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations and the Declaration of Helsinki.
A total of 191 WLHIV were enrolled.
We enrolled women living with HIV to collect primary data on cervical cancer at Connaught Hospital, which is Sierra Leone's national referral hospital with a capacity of 300 beds.

Participants were selected using a systematic random sampling approach, whereby every fourth eligible woman who met the inclusion criteria and provided written informed consent was enrolled in the study.
All study participants provided written informed consent before enrollment and participation.
We recruited 191 HIV-infected women with a modal age group of 25-34 years and a mean age of 231 34.61 years.
All participants were receiving 233 antiretroviral therapy.

These are significantly present in our participants, further solidifying their risk of persistent HPV infection and progression to cervical cancer, in the background of their already immunocompromised state.

Even though all our participants in our study are on highly active antiretroviral therapy, 26.2% of them had treatment interruption, highlighting the need for continuous treatment adherence counseling for both new and old clients, given the benefits of sustained viral suppression.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001. This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold"). ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "P<0.2", Text = "Candidate predictors underwent univariate screening (retaining variables with P<0.2), followed by multicollinearity assessment via variance inflation factors (VIF; sequentially removing variables with VIF>10 until all remaining had VIF≤10), final models were built using backward elimination of remaining variables, reporting adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. ::: *P* values are never exactly zero. A *p* value of .000 is a rounding artifact — the actual value is simply smaller than the reported precision. Very small *p* values should be reported as *p* < .001 rather than *p* = .000. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p = 0.0", Text = "A minimum sample size (n) of 178 was determined using a 95% confidence level (Z = 1.96), a cervical disease prevalence (p) of 0.134 reported in a comparable study conducted in Cambodia, a low-and middle-income country 19, and its complement (q = 1.0 -p = 0.0.866) at a degree of precision (d) of 0.05."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("P<0.2", "p = 0.78"), Sentence = c("Candidate predictors underwent univariate screening (retaining variables with P<0.2), followed by multicollinearity assessment via variance inflation factors (VIF; sequentially removing variables with VIF>10 until all remaining had VIF≤10), final models were built using backward elimination of remaining variables, reporting adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI).", "The Hosmer-Lemeshow test indicated adequate fit (p = 0.78)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Cervical cancer, a malignancy affecting the cervix, is the fourth most common cancer and cause of cancer-related mortality among women worldwide.
This burden disproportionately affects lowresource regions, where approximately 90% of cases occur.
HIV-positive women are at high risk of persistent Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection and cervical cancer, but screening for this cancer is not yet integrated into HIV care in Sierra Leone.
This study aimed to assess the prevalence and risk factors of high-risk HPV infection among women living with HIV (WLHIV) attending Connaught Hospital in Sierra Leone.
We conducted a cross-sectional study of women living with HIV aged 25-65 years attending the HIV clinic at Connaught Teaching Hospital in Freetown between September and December 2024.
Endocervical swabs were collected for HPV DNA testing.
Data was analyzed using R (v4.4.0).
Logistic regression analysis was used to determine the independent risk factors for HPV positivity.
A total of 191 WLHIV were enrolled.
The mean age was 36.8 years; 44.5% were single, and 67% were employed.
High-risk HPV DNA was detected in 60 (31.4%) (95% CI 25.3%-38.3%) participants, with 50% (30/60) having multiple serotypes.
The most common genotype was HPV 52, followed by 16 and 51.
Only 30% of HPV-positive women had genotypes 16 or 18, targeted by the bivalent vaccine.
On multivariable analysis, former contraceptive use was independently associated with increased HPV positivity (aOR=4.86, 95% CI: 1.65-17.37, p = 0.0032).

The high prevalence of high-risk HPV infection and predominance of non 16/18 genotypes among WLHIV in Sierra Leone underscore the need to integrate HPV screening within HIV services and consider broader HPV vaccine coverage in Sierra Leone.
Former contraceptive use is an independent predictor of HPV positivity, emphasizing the need for robust screening strategies in women using contraceptives.
Globally, cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer and the fourth leading cause of cancer death in women, with an estimated 660,000 new cases and 350,000 deaths in 2022 1,2 .

The global cervical cancer deaths are predicted to increase to 460,000 by 2040 without effective preventive interventions. 3 In sub-Saharan Africa, it is the second most common cancer and the leading cause of cancer-related deaths among women 2 .

text.text: There are no prior research data on HPV among women living with HIV in Sierra Leone.
This study aimed to assess the prevalence and risk factors of HPV among women living with HIV at the national referral hospital in Sierra Leone.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study evaluating HPV prevalence and genotype distribution among WLHIV in Sierra Leone.

We employed a cross-sectional study design to screen for HPV in women living with HIV aged 25 to 65, presenting at the Connaught Teaching Hospital's HIV clinic for routine HIV services between September and December 2024.
We enrolled women living with HIV to collect primary data on cervical cancer at Connaught Hospital, which is Sierra Leone's national referral hospital with a capacity of 300 beds.
It is a teaching hospital affiliated with the College of Medicine and Allied Health Sciences of the University of Sierra Leone.
Connaught Hospital's HIV clinic is the largest HIV center in the country and doubles as the country's only referral center for advanced HIV Diseases.
The HIV clinic offers outpatient services to over 7,500 clients as of December 2024.
Out of 7,500, 4,567 (60.9%) were females, of whom 3,197 (42.6%) fell within the 25-65 year age range.
The hospital offers inpatient services for HIV, which accounts for over 40% of all medical admissions 14.

text.text: The first phase of this study is screening for HPV, the results of which have been prepared into this manuscript.
Therefore, we used cervical dysplasia prevalence to calculate the sample size of this study.

Participants were selected using a systematic random sampling approach, whereby every fourth eligible woman who met the inclusion criteria and provided written informed consent was enrolled in the study.
Women aged 25-65 years with confirmed HIV and no history of cervical diseases were eligible for inclusion if they were able and willing to provide written informed consent.

We excluded pregnant women, women with a history of hysterectomy with removal of the cervix (trachelectomy) or prior diagnosis of cervical cancer or ongoing treatment for cervical cancer and women with active menstruation at the time of screening (with eligibility for rescheduling).
We also excluded women with severe acute illness requiring immediate medical attention and those with an inability to provide informed consent due to cognitive impairment or severe illness.
HPV DNA was determined using the High-Risk HPV Typing Nucleic Acid Detection kit (ZJ Biotech, Shanghai, China).
The high-risk HPV genotyping kits demonstrated a limit of detection (LoD) of 1×10⁴ copies/ml (defined via serial dilution of HPV-positive subtype standards).

At this LoD, 10 independent repeated detections for each subtype yielded a 100% detection rate (no false negatives), meeting National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) In vitro Diagnostics registration Criteria.
Analytical performance (LoD determination and reproducibility) was validated per the manufacturer's protocol and NMPA guidelines.
• LoD Determination: Serial dilutions of HPV-positive subtype standards identified the lowest detectable concentration as 1×10⁴ copies/ml.

• Reproducibility: At this LoD, 10 independent repeated detections for each subtype showed a 100% detection rate (no false negatives; ZJ Bio-Tech validation report, 2024), confirming kit reliability for low-concentration samples.
Endocervical swabs were collected by trained clinicians according to standard protocols using a cytobrush and sent for HPV Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) testing.

Endocervical swab samples were processed for DNA extraction using the following protocol: Swabs were placed in 1.5 mL centrifuge tubes containing 1 mL of Lysis Buffer B and incubated at 56°C for 10 minutes.
After incubation, 50 μL of Proteinase K was added, and the samples were further incubated at 56°C for 10 additional minutes.
To precipitate DNA, 400 μL of absolute ethanol was added, followed by gentle mixing and a 5-minute incubation at room temperature.
The mixture was then centrifuged at 13,000 rpm for 5 minutes, and the supernatant was carefully removed.
The DNA pellet was washed with 1 mL of 70% ethanol, recentrifuged at 13,000 rpm for 5 minutes, and the supernatant was discarded.
Each reaction mixture contained 36μL of HPV polymerase chain reaction (PCR) mixture 4μL of supernatant as DNA template.
HPV amplification and detection were performed with the CFX96 real-time PCR detection system (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, California, USA).

A structured, interviewer-administered questionnaire was used to collect socio-demographic data (age, sex, occupation, level of education, history of cigarette smoking and illicit drug use, and marital status) and clinical data (parity, gravidity, use of contraceptives, abortion).
HIV-related information was extracted directly from HIV registers and patients' treatment cards.
The questionnaire was developed in English and administered in the local Krio language to enhance participants' understanding.
Data collection was conducted by trained HIV nurses who were fluent in Krio and familiar with HIV and cervical cancer care protocols.
Statistical analyses were performed using R (R Core Team, Vienna, Austria).
Baseline characteristics were summarized using frequency and percentage (%).
We used Pearson's chisquare and Fisher's exact test to test statistical significance.

Multivariable logistic regression was independently performed for two outcomes (HPV DNA positivity and multiple high-risk serotype co-infection), adjusting for age, education, occupation, marital status and parity.

Candidate predictors underwent univariate screening (retaining variables with P<0.2), followed by multicollinearity assessment via variance inflation factors (VIF; sequentially removing variables with VIF>10 until all remaining had VIF≤10), final models were built using backward elimination of remaining variables, reporting adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI).

Statistical significance was considered with p-value < 0.05.

text.text: The primary outcome variable was high-risk HPV DNA positivity (binary: positive vs negative), defined as the detection of any of the 15 high-risk HPV genotypes by nucleic acid testing.
The secondary outcome was multiple high-risk HPV co-infection, defined as detection of two or more high-risk HPV genotypes.

Explanatory variables included socio-demographic characteristics (age, occupation, educational level, marital status), reproductive-health-related factors (age at first sexual intercourse, parity, age at first childbirth, abortion history and abortion times, contraceptive use status, contraceptive type and duration of contraceptive use), clinical HIV-related variables (HIV diagnosis duration, new patient status, antiretroviral treatment interruption), and behavioural factors (smoking history, alcohol drinking, illicit drug use).
Family history of cancer and personal cancer history were also included as covariates.

text.text: Socio-demographic, behavioural, clinical and reproductive-health data were collected by trained research staff using standardized paper-based questionnaires administered through face-to-face participant interviews.
Endocervical swab specimens were collected using cytobrushes for laboratory HPV-DNA testing.
HPV genotyping was performed with the High-Risk HPV Typing Nucleic Acid Detection kit (ZJ Biotech, Shanghai, China), which could identify 15 high-risk HPV genotypes.
DNA extraction and real-time PCR amplification were performed following the manufacturer's standard laboratory protocols.
Questionnaire variables and laboratory test results were double-entered and cleaned prior to statistical analysis.
Several potential sources of bias were addressed in this study.

To reduce selection bias, we consecutively enrolled every fourth eligible female client attending the HIV clinic to avoid convenience-sampling bias; however, as recruitment was conducted within a single national referral hospital, selection bias could not be fully eliminated and the sample may not represent all women living with HIV across Sierra Leone.
Interview-related information bias was minimised by training interviewers and using a standardised questionnaire.
Laboratory measurement bias was reduced by strictly following standard operating procedures for specimen collection, DNA extraction and PCR detection.
Missing data were minimal in this dataset.

Confounding bias was managed in the analytical stage: univariate screening, variance inflation factor assessment for multicollinearity, and multivariable logistic regression with backward elimination were applied to adjust for potential confounding variables.

text.text: This is the first study assessing the prevalence and risk factors of HPV infection among women living with HIV in Sierra Leone, providing insights on the burden of HPV infection.
Our results report a 31% prevalence of high-risk HPV infections among women living with HIV with more than half of them having more than one genotype.
Also, serotype 52 was detected in 17 (28.3%) participants.
Only 30% of those who tested positive for HPV had either genotype 16 or 18, with one participant having both.
Finally, former use of contraceptives is an independent predictor of HPV DNA positivity.
The high-risk HPV prevalence among women living with HIV (31.4%) from our study is similar to studies in women living with HIV in Europe (30.5-33.9%) 20 and China (30.6%) 21 .

text.text: Similar prevalence rates are reported among the general population in a systematic review in SSA (34%) 22 , and from observational studies in Nigeria (37%) 23 and Ghana (37%) 24 .
text.formatted: Similar prevalence rates are reported among the general population in a systematic review in SSA (34%) <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">22</ref> , and from observational studies in Nigeria (37%) <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">23</ref> and Ghana (37%) <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">24</ref> .

text.text: Furthermore, our high-risk HPV prevalence is higher than reported in Uganda (21%) 25.
text.formatted: Furthermore, our high-risk HPV prevalence is higher than reported in Uganda (21%) <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">25</ref>.

text.text: The high prevalence of high-risk HPV infection among women living with HIV in Sierra Leone reflects the country's substantial burden of HIV and cervical cancer.
Even though the HIV prevalence is 1.7% in Sierra Leone 4, 11 , there is a high burden of advanced HIV disease 13, 14, 26.
text.formatted: Even though the HIV prevalence is 1.7% in Sierra Leone <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr">11</ref> , there is a high burden of advanced HIV disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">26</ref>.

text.text: Cervical cancer is the second most common cancer among women in Sierra Leone, with the country being placed at 22 nd in the world, for the estimated age-adjusted death rate 4 .
text.formatted: Cervical cancer is the second most common cancer among women in Sierra Leone, with the country being placed at 22 nd in the world, for the estimated age-adjusted death rate <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">4</ref> .

text.text: There are limited cervical cancer services in the country, with screening and treatment services available in only 5 of the 16 districts.

Even though the WHO recommends HPV testing as the first-choice method of screening for cervical cancer 17 , Sierra Leone still uses visual inspection with acetic acid in all 15 screening centres in the country 4.

text.text: The main HPV genotypes reported in Eastern and Southern African countries are 16 and 52, whereas 16 and 35 are the main genotypes in Western African countries 27 .
text.formatted: The main HPV genotypes reported in Eastern and Southern African countries are 16 and 52, whereas 16 and 35 are the main genotypes in Western African countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">27</ref> .

text.text: Unlike the reported genotypes across Africa, the commonest genotype in our study is 52, followed by 16 and 51.
This is contrary to a recent systematic review in women living with HIV, which reported 16 as the most common genotype, followed by 18, and 45 28, 29 .
text.formatted: This is contrary to a recent systematic review in women living with HIV, which reported 16 as the most common genotype, followed by 18, and 45 <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">28,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">29</ref> .

text.text: Our study reveals the high prevalence of multiple high-risk HPV infections (50%), higher than in the global report (39.1%) and studies from Africa (22.6%) 29, 30.
text.formatted: Our study reveals the high prevalence of multiple high-risk HPV infections (50%), higher than in the global report (39.1%) and studies from Africa (22.6%) <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">29,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">30</ref>.

text.text: These multiple infections are known to play a significant role in cervical carcinogenesis due to increased persistence/prolonged exposure and high viral load to various types of high-risk HPVs, with possibilities of synergistic oncogenic effects [31] [32] [33] [34].
text.formatted: These multiple infections are known to play a significant role in cervical carcinogenesis due to increased persistence/prolonged exposure and high viral load to various types of high-risk HPVs, with possibilities of synergistic oncogenic effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[31]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[32]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[33]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[34]</ref>.

text.text: Reports have shown that smoking 35, 36 , alcohol [37] [38] [39] , multiparity 40, 41 , use of oral contraceptive pills [41] [42] [43] [44] and early age of sexual debut and first childbirth 45-47 are some notable risk factors for persistent HPV infection and cervical cancer.
text.formatted: Reports have shown that smoking <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">36</ref> , alcohol <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[37]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[38]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[39]</ref> , multiparity <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">40,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">41</ref> , use of oral contraceptive pills <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[41]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[42]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[43]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">[44]</ref> and early age of sexual debut and first childbirth 45-47 are some notable risk factors for persistent HPV infection and cervical cancer.

text.text: These are significantly present in our participants, further solidifying their risk of persistent HPV infection and progression to cervical cancer, in the background of their already immunocompromised state.

The lack of a statistically significant association between high-risk HPV genotypes and factors like smoking, alcohol use, and early sexual debut, contrary to other studies 35, 37, 41 , could be attributed to variations in sample size, methodological differences, or population characteristics.

text.text: Highly active antiretroviral therapy has been shown to reduce the incidence and progression of lesions in women living with HIV 48, 49 .
text.formatted: Highly active antiretroviral therapy has been shown to reduce the incidence and progression of lesions in women living with HIV <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">48,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">49</ref> .

text.text: Even though all our participants in our study are on highly active antiretroviral therapy, 26.2% of them had treatment interruption, highlighting the need for continuous treatment adherence counseling for both new and old clients, given the benefits of sustained viral suppression.
Cervical cancer is preventable and highly treatable when detected early.
Generally, cervical cancer screening in women living with HIV is low in SSA; (30%) 50 .
text.formatted: Generally, cervical cancer screening in women living with HIV is low in SSA; (30%) <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">50</ref> .

text.text: The negligible uptake identified in our study is alarming, considering their significant risk of developing cervical cancer, as it represents a missed opportunity for early intervention, especially in a low resource setting like ours.
Our study reports that former use of oral contraceptives is an independent predictor of increased HPV positivity and the presence of multiple genotypes in women living with HIV.

The use of hormonal contraceptives has been linked to oncogenesis and HPV persistence, likely due to hormonal effects on cervical endothelial changes, highlighting the importance of robust screening strategies for early detection and management of cervical cancer in women taking these contraceptives 51.
text.formatted: The use of hormonal contraceptives has been linked to oncogenesis and HPV persistence, likely due to hormonal effects on cervical endothelial changes, highlighting the importance of robust screening strategies for early detection and management of cervical cancer in women taking these contraceptives <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">51</ref>.

text.text: Sierra Leone has piloted HPV vaccination in adolescent girls, with over 150,000 girls vaccinated.
The vaccine used was a bivalent vaccine targeting HPV genotypes 16 and 18 4 .
text.formatted: The vaccine used was a bivalent vaccine targeting HPV genotypes 16 and 18 <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">4</ref> .

text.text: The 5 most common genotypes from our study were 52, 16, 51, 35, 39, and 58, justifying the need for quadrivalent or, better still, a nonvalent HPV vaccine with a high HPV genotype coverage.
Connaught Teaching Hospital's HIV clinic, Sierra Leone's national HIV referral centre, does not have structures for cervical cancer screening.

As integration of cervical cancer services into routine HIV care has been shown to improve the quality of life of women living with HIV, 52 we hope that these findings highlighted from our study will inform decisions and policies on implementation and integration of cervical cancer services in ART clinics in Sierra Leone.
text.formatted: As integration of cervical cancer services into routine HIV care has been shown to improve the quality of life of women living with HIV, <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">52</ref> we hope that these findings highlighted from our study will inform decisions and policies on implementation and integration of cervical cancer services in ART clinics in Sierra Leone.

text.text: Our study has limitations-it is a single-center study with a small sample size of 191 women living with HIV in a national referral hospital; thus, its findings are not representative of the HPV status in Sierra Leone.
The high-risk HPV typing nucleic acid detection kit used in this study has a higher LoD of 1×10⁴ copies/ml.
This may have underestimated the prevalence of high-risk HPV genotype in this population.
Again, we did not measure CD4 cell count and assess its impact on HPV positivity.
Despite this limitation, this study has clinical and public health relevance as it provides the first evidence of HPV in Sierra Leone.

We report a high prevalence (31%) of high-risk HPV genotypes among women living with HIV in Sierra Leone, dominated by genotype 52, which is different from those protected against using the bivalent vaccines.

The high prevalence of high-risk HPV and predominance of non 16/18 genotypes underscore the need for integrating HPV screening into HIV care, and introducing broader-spectrum vaccination (nonavalent vaccines) could substantially reduce cervical cancer risk among women living with HIV in Sierra Leone.

Furthermore, we observed that former oral contraceptive use is an independent predictor of increased high-risk HPV positivity and the presence of multiple high-risk HPV genotypes, emphasizing the need for robust screening strategies for women on contraceptives.
